clue.text: Delight for mad cats? Yes!

indicators.note: something mad is deranged, so the letters that follow are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cat lover cheers at the thought of crazy cats bringing joy.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecstasy is an overwhelming feeling of happiness, a strong synonym for great pleasure.

clue.text: Be capable of potty dance

blocks.note: to be able to do something
the can is slang for a toilet, as is a potty

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether they could manage a silly little dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potty' reads as an adjective meaning crazy, but here it is the noun: a child's toilet, or in slang the can. CANCAN is the high-kicking French dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The cancan is a lively, high-kicking French music-hall routine performed by chorus lines.

clue.text: Stop twerp undressing in part of castle

indicators.note: undressing strips the outer layers away, so each word loses its first and last letters

blocks.note: the word stripped of its outer letters
the word stripped of its outer letters

explanation.surface: An order to a silly young man to stop taking his clothes off in a castle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undressing' applies to both stop and twerp, leaving TO and WER.
explanation.definitionFit: A tower is a tall structure forming one section of a fortified castle, such as a keep or turret.

clue.text: Loyalty for Proust admitting penny dreadful

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so the novelist's name takes another letter inside it
dreadful means very bad, signalling the combined letters must be put into a different order

blocks.note: Marcel Proust, the French novelist, taken as written
p is the abbreviation for a penny

explanation.surface: A cheap sensational novel (a penny dreadful) is found inside Proust, testing a reader's loyalty.
explanation.walkthrough: A penny dreadful was a cheap Victorian thriller magazine; the phrase is split here, penny giving P and dreadful the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Support means backing or allegiance given to a person or cause, close in sense to loyalty.

clue.text: Unfairly blames husband for awkward gait

indicators.note: unfairly suggests something not done properly, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A wife unjustly blames her husband for his clumsy way of walking.
explanation.definitionFit: A shamble is a slow, clumsy, shuffling way of walking, a noun for an ungainly manner of moving.

clue.text: Expression of joy could be the last

blocks.note: a cheer or shout of delight
completes the idiom for a final flourish or farewell performance before retiring

explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives a plain definition and then hints at the phrase 'the last ...', meaning a final effort at the end of a career.
explanation.definitionFit: A hurrah is a shout of triumph or approval, and the last one is a final hurrah before bowing out.

clue.text: Man-made or plastic notes

indicators.note: plastic material can be moulded into any shape, so these letters are remoulded

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the hyphen

explanation.surface: Synthetic materials, whether artificial or plastic, are being contrasted, like an office supplies catalogue.
explanation.definitionFit: Memoranda is the plural of memorandum, written messages or reminders circulated in an office.

clue.text: I go and call afresh, being reasonable

indicators.note: doing something afresh means starting again in a new way, so the letters are set out anew

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sensibly goes back and phones again.
explanation.definitionFit: Logical describes thinking that follows sound reasoning, so it is a close synonym for sensible or rational.

clue.text: Change law or gambling could get us all heated up?

indicators.note: to change something is to alter it, so these letters are altered into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A debate over gambling laws threatens to make everyone angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heated up' looks like anger at a gambling law, but it is literal: the whole planet warming, and 'Change' doubles as a nod to climate change.
explanation.definitionFit: Global warming is the rise in Earth's average temperature, literally making the whole planet and everyone on it hotter.

clue.text: Nag daft wife and cause distress

indicators.note: daft means silly or crazy, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: Pestering a foolish wife only makes her unhappy.
explanation.definitionFit: To gnaw, figuratively, is to worry or torment someone persistently, as anxiety gnaws at the mind.

clue.text: Trip from drug — mostly horrid time

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the word before it loses its final letter

blocks.note: a pill is a tablet of medicine
grim means unpleasant or dreadful
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A drug-induced trip turned into a long, unpleasant experience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trip' tempts a drugs reading alongside 'drug', but it means a journey.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilgrimage is a journey to a sacred place, so trip works as a looser synonym for such travel.

clue.text: Mark a bit of headscarf

indicators.note: a bit of means only a portion of the following word is taken, sitting inside it

blocks.note: the letters run consecutively inside this word

explanation.surface: Someone points to a small stain on part of a headscarf.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is a lasting mark left on the skin after a wound heals, so mark is a fair synonym.

clue.text: See 2
Pair accepts ongoing army training to begin with for Thames battle

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so the word for a pair holds other letters inside it
to begin with points at the opening letter of each of the preceding words

blocks.note: a brace is a pair, especially of game birds
the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: A couple of soldiers in continuing training prepare for a clash on the Thames.
explanation.walkthrough: The Boat Race is the annual rowing contest between Oxford and Cambridge universities on the River Thames in London.
explanation.definitionFit: The Boat Race is a fiercely fought rowing contest held on the London river, hence a battle on the water.

clue.text: Trendy cool hat is childish

blocks.note: in means fashionable
to fan is to cool something down
tile is old slang for a hat

explanation.surface: Wearing a supposedly fashionable hat is called immature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cool' looks like a synonym of trendy, but it is a verb here: to fan. Tile is dated slang for a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Infantile means behaving like a baby or small child, so it is a direct synonym for childish.

clue.text: School mums involved in reform

indicators.note: being involved in something means being caught up inside it, so one word goes within another

blocks.note: to alter is to change or reform
ma is mother, so two of them for the plural

explanation.surface: Mothers campaign to change a school.
explanation.definitionFit: One's alma mater is the school or university one attended, Latin for nourishing mother.

clue.text: Fish can be obtuse

definitions.note: an example: an obtuse one is wider than a right one

blocks.note: first meaning: to fish with rod and line
second meaning: a geometric figure between two lines that may exceed ninety degrees

explanation.surface: A dim-witted fish is being described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obtuse' suggests a stupid fish, but here it is the geometry term for an angle greater than ninety degrees.
explanation.definitionFit: To angle is to fish with a hook and line, and in geometry an angle wider than a right angle is called obtuse.

clue.text: Silly Superman ran out of froth

indicators.note: here the clue's own word ran is taken out of the superhero's name
silly means foolish or scrambled, so what is left is rearranged

blocks.note: the comic-book hero, taken as written

explanation.surface: A foolish Superman has run short of foam.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'ran' does double duty: it is both the letters removed and part of the instruction 'out of', leaving SUPEM to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Spume is the foam that forms on waves or liquid, so froth is an exact synonym.

clue.text: Pretend drug put down bog, in the main

indicators.note: in the main means for the most part, so only most of the preceding word is used

blocks.note: to place something is to put it down
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone flushed fake medication down the toilet at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the main' suggests the sea, but means mostly, so bog loses its last letter. A bog is British slang for a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A placebo is an inactive substance given as if it were medicine, so a pretend drug describes it well.

clue.text: Janitor finding joyrider around the middle of Leeds

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece wraps the other
the middle of picks out the central letter of the city's name

blocks.note: a joyrider takes a car, so is literally a car taker
the central letter of the five-letter city name

explanation.surface: A school caretaker catches a car thief in Leeds.
explanation.walkthrough: Joyrider is read whimsically as 'car taker', someone who steals cars to drive for fun. Leeds is a city in Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: A caretaker looks after a building and its maintenance, the British equivalent of a janitor.

clue.text: In speech I'd name an egg-laying mammal

indicators.note: in tells the solver the answer sits inside the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the word boundaries

explanation.surface: A speaker announces they will name an unusual animal in their talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In speech' suggests a sound-alike clue, but 'In' alone is the signal and the letters are concealed in the words.
explanation.definitionFit: The echidna, or spiny anteater, is one of the rare monotremes, mammals that lay eggs.

clue.text: Insect's shell-like rug?

blocks.note: shell-like is British slang for the ear, from its shape
a rug is slang for a toupee or hairpiece

explanation.surface: An insect has a carpet resembling a seashell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A word in your shell-like' is British slang for a word in your ear, and a rug is a slang name for a wig.
explanation.definitionFit: The earwig is a small insect with pincers at the end of its body.

clue.text: Quiet order became smaller

blocks.note: sh is the call for silence
a rank is a position in an order or hierarchy

explanation.surface: A calm, orderly arrangement got reduced in size.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrank is the past tense of shrink, meaning to reduce in size or contract.

clue.text: Meat provided by standard mother (one who overacts)

blocks.note: par is the normal or expected standard
ma is an informal word for mother
a ham is an actor who overplays a part

explanation.surface: A melodramatic mother supplies the usual cold cuts.
explanation.definitionFit: Parma ham is a cured Italian prosciutto from the Parma region, a type of cold meat.

clue.text: Reportedly go off bird

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is said or heard, so the word is identified by its sound

blocks.note: milk that goes off is said to turn sour

explanation.surface: Word has it that a bird has gone bad.
explanation.definitionFit: The tern is a slender seabird related to gulls, with forked tail and pointed wings.

clue.text: Step off around axis of sorts

indicators.note: off suggests something wrong or out of place, so the letters are rearranged
around means the jumbled letters enclose another piece

blocks.note: taken as written
y is a standard name for a graph axis

explanation.surface: Someone moves off a pivot point of some kind.
explanation.walkthrough: The x and y axes are the two lines of a graph, so axis can give either letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Types and sorts are both words for kinds or categories of things.

clue.text: Nap, then shower — editor's calm!

blocks.note: a rest is a short sleep
a shower is a fall of rain
ed is the abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: After a nap and a shower, the newspaper editor is relaxed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shower' suggests a wash, but here it is a light fall of rain.
explanation.definitionFit: Restrained means self-controlled and unexcited, so calm describes a restrained manner well.

clue.text: Change over hands

indicators.note: over suggests turning something over, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: to swap is to exchange or change

explanation.surface: It is time to switch which hand is doing the work.
explanation.definitionFit: Paws is informal for human hands, borrowed from the word for animal feet.

clue.text: See 22
Get over Brexit rapidly or Kent's economic leaders lose their shirts

indicators.note: leaders are those at the front, so the first letter of each word is taken

blocks.clueFragment: Get over Brexit rapidly or Kent's economic
blocks.note: the opening letter of each of these words

explanation.surface: Unless the country moves on from leaving the EU fast, business leaders in Kent face ruin.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent is a county in south-east England near the Channel ports, where Brexit trade disruption was keenly felt.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose one's shirt is an idiom for losing all one's money, which is what going broke means.

clue.text: A guess? A cuckoo? A dog?

indicators.note: cuckoo means crazy, so the letters before it are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring punctuation

explanation.surface: A quiz host fires off wild guesses about birds and dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cuckoo' looks like a bird in a list with dog, but it is the anagram signal. Dog is slang for a sausage, as in hot dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot dog is a sausage in a bun, so dog serves as informal shorthand for a sausage.
